transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello Ms. Osei, I am Dr. Miller. I am the resident on the team. I wanted to sit down with you today to discuss why your symptoms have returned and look at your chart again.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you for seeing me. I was quite surprised to feel the fever and the pain coming back after I thought I'd finished the course.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have the records here. I reviewed the prescription that was sent over last time, and the issue is that you were prescribed the correct medication and the correct dose, but the duration was only for seven days when it should have been fourteen.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait. Seven days?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes. The prescription was written for half the time required to fully clear the infection.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I see. As a nurse practitioner, I know that an incomplete course essentially leaves the door open for a relapse. I noticed the bottle said seven days, but I assumed that was the clinical decision based on my presentation.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Does that make sense in terms of why you are feeling sick again?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It makes perfect sense. But this is a fundamental prescribing error.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Right. Now, the clinic was extremely understaffed that week and there were a lot of overlapping orders in the system.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I am less interested in the staffing levels and more concerned with the standard of care. A fourteen-day course is standard for this diagnosis. Why was this missed?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was just a clerical oversight during the entry process.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: An oversight. That is a very clinical way to describe something that has put me back in a hospital bed.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can tell you are frustrated.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Frustrated is one word. I am concerned about the lack of oversight. Who checked the prescription?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I think we can just move on to how we fix this now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't think we can just move on. I expect a level of professional accountability here.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Look, it was a mistake. These things happen in a busy environment.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: They happen, but they shouldn't. I would have caught it if I weren't feeling so ill, but I trusted the provider's order.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have to get to another patient in a few minutes, so let's just focus on the next steps.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You are rushing me through the fact that you gave me the wrong amount of medicine.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am just trying to be efficient.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Efficient is not the same as professional. This is a breach of basic safety standards.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. But really, the dose was correct, so it isn't like you were given a toxic amount.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is not the point. The point is that the treatment was incomplete.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Right. So, for the plan, I'm going to get you a new prescription for the remaining seven days of the antibiotic.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And when will that be processed?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Sometime today. You can probably pick it up at the pharmacy this evening.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Will there be any change in the medication or just the duration?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Just the duration. You'll finish the full fourteen days.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what is being done to make sure this doesn't happen to the next person?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will look into it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is a very vague answer.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is just how the system works. We'll put a note in the file.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not satisfied with that. I would expect a formal incident report to be filed.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I really have to go now. Just take the new pills and you should be fine.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I will take the pills, but I want to know who is supervising your prescribing.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That can be discussed later. Just check the pharmacy later today.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('I have to get to another patient', 'I really have to go now') and shows defensive escalation under pushback.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the second turn, lay language was used, and comprehension was checked once ('Does that make sense...').

A.justification: No direct apology language was used, and responsibility was deflected to staffing levels and clerical oversight.

R.justification: Resident uses generic validation ('I can tell you are frustrated', 'I understand') but otherwise meets emotional bids with factual redirection.

T.justification: Resident provides a specific next step (new prescription) with a timeline (today/this evening) and a patient role (pick it up at the pharmacy).
